extracted.intended_audience: law students, patent practitioners, and interested public
extracted.subtask_description: Summarize the legal standards and multi-jurisdictional tests used to determine whether a variant not literally within a patent claim nonetheless infringes under the doctrine of equivalents. Covers Germany, Switzerland, UK, US, EPC/WIPO harmonization attempts, and related limits/defenses.

rubrics_metrics.name: Schneidmesser three-step test (Germany)
rubrics_metrics.description: German courts typically apply a three-step test known as Schneidmesser's questions:
rubrics_metrics.guidance:
The three questions (as stated):
1) Does the variant solve the problem underlying the invention with means that objectively have the same effect?
2) Would the person skilled in the art, using the common general knowledge, have realised at the priority date that the variant has the same effect?
3) Are the considerations which the skilled person takes into account for the variant in the light of the meaning of the invention close enough to the considerations taken into account for the literal solution protected by the claims, such that the skilled person will consider the variant as a solution which is equivalent to the literal one?
All of the above questions need to be answered in the affirmative in order to demonstrate equivalent infringement. In addition, an allegation of equivalent infringement in Germany needs to withstand the Formstein test (see separate entry).

rubrics_metrics.name: Formstein test (Germany) — defence limiting equivalence
rubrics_metrics.description: Corresponding question in Germany (Formstein): Does the variant, having regard to the state of the art, lack novelty or is the variant obvious to a person skilled in the art?
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If the variant is not novel or is obvious in light of the prior art, the Formstein defence can prevent a finding of equivalent infringement. The Formstein test operates as a check against expanding protection to subject-matter that would be anticipated or obvious.

rubrics_metrics.name: Swiss three-prong test (Switzerland)
rubrics_metrics.description: Federal Patent Court of Switzerland adopted an approach similar to the German three-prong test, asking three questions:
rubrics_metrics.guidance:
The three questions (as used by the Swiss court):
1) Do the replaced features have the same objective function (same effect)?
2) Are the replaced features and their same objective function obvious to a person skilled in the art on the basis of the teaching of the patent (accessibility)?
3) After reading the wording of the claim in light of the description, would a person skilled in the art consider the replaced features as a solution of equal value (equal value)?
Guidance/examples: Swiss decisions applied these questions to deny or find equivalence (e.g., denial where patent teaching explicitly allowed replacement of toxic chromium by metallic catalysts and the alternative TEMPO was not a solution of equal value; finding of equivalence where replacement was basic undergraduate knowledge). The Federal Supreme Court has affirmed the approach in later cases but may analyze embodiments and 'key teachings' of the patent.

rubrics_metrics.name: Purposive construction (UK/Catnic)
rubrics_metrics.description: UK courts moved from literal/textual infringement to a 'purposive construction' of patent claims: the question is whether a skilled person reading the patent would understand that strict compliance with a word or phrase within the claim was intended by the patentee to be an essential requirement.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Purposive construction balances literal claim wording against patent description and drawings to avoid purely literalism and to identify which claim terms are essential. It underpins later UK approaches (Improver/Protocol questions and the Actavis formulation).

rubrics_metrics.name: Improver/Protocol questions (UK historical three-step test)
rubrics_metrics.description: A three-step test (the 'Improver' or 'Protocol' questions) became widely used in the UK to determine non-literal infringement prior to the Actavis reform.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The Improver questions provided a structured means of assessing whether a variant was equivalent to a claimed element. (The Wikipedia entry notes these questions became stable with Improver v Remington and Kirin-Amgen decisions, but does not reproduce their exact wording here.)

rubrics_metrics.name: Actavis / UK Supreme Court three questions (2017)
rubrics_metrics.description: The Supreme Court in Actavis UK v Eli Lilly revised the UK test for non-literal infringement to the following three questions:
rubrics_metrics.guidance:
The Actavis questions (verbatim):
1) 'Notwithstanding that it is not within the literal meaning of the relevant claim(s) of the patent, does the variant achieve substantially the same result in substantially the same way as the invention, ie the inventive concept revealed by the patent?'
2) 'Would it be obvious to the person skilled in the art, reading the patent at the priority date, but knowing that the variant achieves substantially the same result as the invention, that it does so in substantially the same way as the invention?'
3) 'Would such a reader of the patent have concluded that the patentee nonetheless intended that strict compliance with the literal meaning of the relevant claim(s) of the patent was an essential requirement of the invention?'
Establishing non-literal infringement requires answers: first two = 'yes' and third = 'no'. The EPC 2000 Protocol amendment was cited as requiring courts to take account of equivalents, influencing this approach.

rubrics_metrics.name: 35 U.S.C. § 112 ¶ 6 statutory equivalents (means-plus-function) (United States)
rubrics_metrics.description: The United States has a statutory equivalents doctrine codified in 35 U.S.C. § 112 ¶ 6, which extends to equivalents available at the patent's issuance and applies to means-plus-function claims.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Means-plus-function claims under §112¶6 are construed to cover the corresponding structure, material, or acts described in the specification and equivalents. The statutory regime limits how equivalents are assessed for such claim language.

rubrics_metrics.name: Judicial doctrine of equivalents (United States — Warner-Jenkinson / triple-identity)
rubrics_metrics.description: The US judicial doctrine of equivalents (non-statutory) extends to technological equivalents developed after the patent is granted and is applied to individual claim limitations. The legal test (Warner-Jenkinson Co. v. Hilton Davis Chem. Co.) asks whether the difference is 'insubstantial.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance:
One way to assess 'insubstantial' difference is the 'triple identity' test: the accused feature
- performs substantially the same function,
- in substantially the same way,
- to obtain the same result
as the limitation literally recited in the claim. The doctrine also applies when two elements are interchangeable and a person of ordinary skill in the art would have known they were interchangeable at the time of infringement. The doctrine operates limitation-by-limitation (not to the invention as a whole).

rubrics_metrics.name: Prosecution history estoppel (United States — limit on equivalents)
rubrics_metrics.description: Prosecution history estoppel prevents a patentee from recapturing through equivalents subject-matter that was surrendered during patent prosecution by amendment or argument narrowing claim scope.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If the patentee abandoned certain literal claim coverage by amending claims during prosecution (e.g., narrowing), the patentee is estopped from later arguing that the surrendered coverage is insubstantially different from the literally claimed limitation. This limits the reach of the doctrine of equivalents.

rubrics_metrics.name: Ensnarement / prior-art limitation (United States)
rubrics_metrics.description: The doctrine of equivalents cannot be used to assert a scope of equivalency that would encompass, or 'ensnare', the prior art.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Courts will reject an equivalents theory if it would cover earlier-known subject-matter because allowing such an equivalence would improperly extend patent protection over what was already in the public domain.

rubrics_metrics.name: Public dedication / disclosure dedication rule (United States)
rubrics_metrics.description: A patentee may not invoke the doctrine of equivalents to recapture subject matter that was disclosed in the patent specification but not claimed (public dedication principle).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Material that was described in the specification but expressly or implicitly left unclaimed is treated as dedicated to the public and cannot later be reclaimed by equivalents arguments.

rubrics_metrics.name: WIPO Basic Proposal Article 21(2) equivalents test (harmonization attempt)
rubrics_metrics.description: WIPO's 1991 'Basic Proposal' for a Treaty Supplementing the Paris Convention proposed that a claim shall cover equivalents and set out two alternative conditions under which an element is generally considered equivalent:
rubrics_metrics.guidance:
The two conditions (as quoted):
(b)(i) 'the equivalent element performs substantially the same function in substantially the same way and produces substantially the same result as the element as expressed in the claim,' or
(b)(ii) 'it is obvious to a person skilled in the art that the same result as that achieved by means of the element as expressed in the claim can be achieved by means of the equivalent element.'
This proposal illustrates harmonization attempts but is not binding international law.

rubrics_metrics.name: EPC 2000 Protocol on the Interpretation of Article 69 (European approach to equivalents)
rubrics_metrics.description: EPC 2000 amended the Protocol on the Interpretation of Article 69 to require courts of contracting states to take due account when considering infringement 'of any element which is an equivalent to an element specified in the claims.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The Protocol amendment instructs courts to consider equivalents when determining extent of protection but did not define 'equivalent', so national courts retain interpretive freedom; the amendment aimed to foster uniformity but its lack of a binding definition limits harmonization.
